Before we go on, I want everyone to commit to an answer. Which figure at the table is Matthew?
The bearded man pointing at himself. He looks as if he is asking, "Who, me?"
That is the traditional reading. Some historians argue it is actually the young man at the end of the table, the one who will not look up.
Really? But then the gesture would mean something completely different.
Exactly. If the young man is Matthew, the bearded man is pointing at him, not at himself.
Then it is the young man who is refusing the call, at least for a second. That makes it much more disquieting.
Does the light help you decide?
Not really. What the light does is connect the hand in the doorway to the whole table. It illuminates everyone.
I have taught this painting for three years and I still change my mind about it every semester.
So the right answer on the assignment is not a name. It is an argument.

Welcome, everyone, and please step a little closer to the chapel on the left. Before you look at anything, you'll need a coin. There's a small box on the wall, and when you drop a coin in, the lights come on for a few minutes. Without it the chapel is simply too dark to see the paintings, which is, in a way, the best introduction to Caravaggio you could ask for. Now look at the canvas on the left wall. That is The Calling of Saint Matthew, and I want you to notice where the light comes from. It enters from the upper right and falls across the faces at the table. Many visitors point out that it seems to come from the direction of the chapel's real window, as if the daylight in this church were entering the picture. Now look at the room itself. It is not a temple or a palace. It is a smoky room full of tax collectors, two of them dressed like fashionable young men of the city. In 1600, showing a sacred moment in a place that looked like an ordinary tavern shocked a good number of viewers. The lights will go off in a moment, so look quickly.

Last week we looked at Caravaggio himself. Today I want to talk about what happened after him, because his story has a strange shape. His influence spread astonishingly fast. Within twenty years painters from Naples to Utrecht were using his dramatic light, his ordinary models and his dark backgrounds. And yet, after his death, his own reputation faded for a very long time, and for centuries many writers treated him as a talented but vulgar painter. Among the artists who absorbed his lessons, three are worth remembering today. Artemisia Gentileschi used the same violent contrasts, but she told stories, often about women, from a perspective that very few painters had given them. Georges de La Tour, in France, turned the beam of light into a single candle and made darkness feel quiet rather than violent. And the young Rembrandt, who never went to Italy, learned the language of shadow from painters who had. Art historians often call these followers the Caravaggisti. The term is useful, but I find it slightly misleading, because it suggests copying. The best of them borrowed his light in order to say something entirely their own.
